blocks.text: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
A protest that blocked routes to the Port of Dover caused hours of disruption, while officials gave differing accounts of the police response.

items: Hundreds of masked men blocked roads near Dover on Saturday, disrupting access to the port and causing miles of tailbacks.
Dover council leader Kevin Mills said police were slow to keep roads open; Kent Police has not commented on the criticism.
The protest lasted from about 07:00 to 11:30 BST, and police said no arrests were made.

blocks.text: Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, said demonstrators had caught several agencies unprepared. He described the protest as exceptionally well organised and said the response appeared slow, while acknowledging that police resources were stretched.
“The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen.”

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds gave a different assessment, saying officers had dealt with the protest swiftly. He condemned what he called intimidatory behaviour and said people in and around Dover had been disrupted.

Mills said the council had received further complaints from villagers in Preston, where protesters appeared to have parked vehicles before travelling into Dover. A Conservative council group leader previously said some demonstrators had arrived in rental vans.

Kent Police described the event as a spontaneous protest and said on Saturday that there had been no arrests. The force has not commented on the council leader's criticism or on who organised the demonstration.

Hope Not Hate said the Patriot Platform network arranged the protest and brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country. Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas praised it online. Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe also said his party supported people protesting against illegal immigration, while describing balaclavas as undesirable.
The protest caused major disruption around Dover, but accounts differ over how quickly police responded and whether the event was spontaneous or organised in advance.

blocks.text: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
A council leader says agencies were caught unprepared when a masked demonstration disrupted access to the Port of Dover. Police have described the protest as spontaneous and made no arrests.

Hundreds of men blocked roads near Dover on Saturday, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port. The demonstration, which lasted from about 07:00 to 11:30 BST, involved chants including “stop the boats”.
“The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen.”

Kevin Mills, leader of Dover District Council, told the BBC that the protest was “exceptionally well organised” and that several agencies had been caught “on the hoof”. He said police appeared slow to keep roads and communication networks open, while acknowledging that police resources were stretched.

Mills said the council had received complaints that protesters appeared to have parked vehicles in the nearby village of Preston before travelling into Dover. The leader of the council’s Conservative group had previously said some men arrived in rental vans.
Kent Police has not commented on the criticism or on who organised the demonstration. On Saturday, the force said officers had made no arrests and described the event as spontaneous.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said officers had dealt with the protest swiftly. He condemned what he called intimidatory behaviour and said people living and travelling around Dover had been disrupted.

The anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate said the Patriot Platform network arranged the protest, bringing together members of anti-migrant groups from across the country. Demonstrators declined to speak to the BBC, although some shouted anti-immigration slogans.

Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas praised the protest on X. Rupert Lowe, the Great Yarmouth MP and leader of Restore Britain, also said his party supported those protesting against illegal immigration, while describing the use of balaclavas as undesirable.

The immediate dispute is over whether the protest was spontaneous and swiftly managed, or organised enough that authorities should have been better prepared. Dover District Council says a formal review is needed; police have yet to respond to that criticism.

blocks.text: Minister to meet JLR boss as thousands of job cuts are expected
Jonathan Reynolds will meet Jaguar Land Rover and Unite leaders to discuss voluntary redundancies, after the company was hit by a costly cyber-attack and weaker sales.

items: JLR has opened a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management staff.
The company has not confirmed the scale of the cuts; reports suggest as many as 4,000 jobs could be affected.
The government says it will discuss long-term investment, but has ruled out a bailout.

blocks.text: Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds is due to meet Jaguar Land Rover bosses and the Unite union early next week. The talks will focus on ways to reduce the impact of expected job losses at the car maker, which employs about 30,000 people in the UK.

JLR confirmed that it has opened a voluntary redundancy programme, a year after a cyber-attack halted production for more than a month. The company said the changes would simplify the business, improve efficiency and build resilience. It did not rule out compulsory redundancies.
“We need to make sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible.”

The Times reported that as many as 4,000 jobs could be lost, largely among white-collar workers, because of tariffs and falling sales. JLR has not confirmed that figure. In July, it said fewer than 300 people would leave under cost-saving plans announced then.

Reynolds said there would be no government support simply to bail out the company, but left open the possibility of long-term investment. He has also discussed support for JLR and its staff with West Midlands mayor Richard Parker.

The company is still recovering from the September 2025 cyber-attack, which stopped all manufacturing for several weeks. Analysts estimated the combined cost of the attack and lost production at £1.9bn. JLR later announced plans to cut about £1.7bn in costs.

The discussions also come as the government considers changes to the electric vehicle sales target. Manufacturers must increase the share of zero-emission vehicles they sell, reaching 80% by 2030. Reynolds said the rules should better reflect consumer demand and current industry conditions.
JLR has confirmed voluntary redundancies but not the number of jobs at risk. The government is offering discussions about competitiveness and investment, rather than a direct bailout.

blocks.text: US envoys arrive in Ukraine after talks with Putin
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in Kyiv after discussions in Moscow about possible next steps towards ending the war.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday, a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. White House officials said the talks covered substantive plans for what comes next, although the details have not been made public.
The visit is the first by President Donald Trump's top negotiators to the Ukrainian capital. An announcement is expected in the coming weeks as diplomatic efforts gather pace.
Both sides described the Moscow meeting in broadly positive terms, while offering few specifics.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he and his team were ready for talks. He said peace would require security guarantees and a coordinated, substantive and realistic approach.
Putin and Zelensky have agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days. The limited pause comes as Russian and Ukrainian forces continue exchanging attacks elsewhere.

Ukraine said its forces struck an oil refinery, an airfield and two air-defence systems in Russia. Russia's defence ministry said the attacks targeted the Ryazan refinery, which supplies the Russian army, and an airfield in Rostov-on-Don.

Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles overnight. It reported that air defences brought down 82 drones and six missiles, while 11 locations were hit and debris fell at seven others.

The Moscow meeting lasted three hours and was held behind closed doors at Putin's official residence, according to Russian state media. Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov called it constructive and extremely frank. He said the discussions included the war, economic issues and possible Russian-American projects.

Ushakov also said the talks addressed what Russia describes as the root causes of the conflict and noted the Russian army's advances. Those remarks come against the backdrop of a war in which Russia controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory, while its ground forces have generally made slow advances at a heavy cost.
The route taken by the envoys from Moscow to Kyiv was not immediately clear. Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The meetings mark a new diplomatic contact between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, but the central proposals and the prospects for a wider agreement remain unclear.

blocks.text: Femi Koleoso: hope can carry us from pain to renewal
The Ezra Collective bandleader guest-edits the Guardian’s culture section, sharing a case for optimism and highlighting the music, films and places that bring him joy.

items: Koleoso grew up in Enfield, began playing drums at church and was supported by state schools and youth clubs.
He describes hope as the belief that renewal and joy can follow pain, even when the timing is unclear.
Ezra Collective members share cultural picks including Rosa Passos, KeiyaA, Southbank Centre and two films.

blocks.text: Koleoso introduces himself plainly: he is a north London musician, drummer, DJ and broadcaster, not a writer or intellectual. He credits his Nigerian family, the UK’s state school system and youth clubs with helping shape a career that has taken him around the world with Ezra Collective.

His guest edit is built around a positive argument. Koleoso recognises the reasons people may feel pessimistic about the UK and the wider world, but says joy remains central to his outlook. For him, hope is not the denial of pain; it is the belief that people can eventually find solid ground.
“On the other side of pain there can be renewal.”

Music is his clearest example. He points to songs shaped by political violence, poverty and historical trauma that nevertheless create movement, connection and joy. Fela Kuti, grime and calypso each show how difficult experiences can produce powerful cultural expression.

The rest of the guest edit follows that route from pain towards joy, with stories and recommendations from Koleoso and his bandmates. Koleoso highlights the Southbank Centre’s steelpan celebrations, where different generations and communities gathered to dance and listen together.

The band’s wider picks include Kleber Mendonça Filho’s film The Secret Agent, Akinola Davies Jr’s My Father’s Shadow, Rosa Passos’s album Recriação and KeiyaA’s Hooke’s Law. Together, they reflect the group’s interest in music, film, cultural identity and the energy created when people experience art collectively.
Koleoso’s message is straightforward: hope does not erase suffering, but it can make renewal feel possible—and art can help people move towards it.

blocks.text: ‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Femi Koleoso on holding on to hope
The Ezra Collective bandleader guest-edits the Saturday culture section, sharing a personal case for optimism and inviting his bandmates to name the work that brings them joy.

When Femi Koleoso was asked to guest-edit the culture section, his first instinct was delight — and a call to his father and former English teacher. The musician jokes that the opportunity places him in an intellectual bracket beyond his wildest dreams, but beneath the humour is genuine pride.

Koleoso describes himself plainly: a drummer, DJ, broadcaster and musician from north London, born to Nigerian parents and raised in Enfield. He began playing drums at church, found encouragement in the state-school system and youth clubs, and now travels the world with Ezra Collective while working in radio and production.
“On the other side of pain there can be renewal.”

His optimism is not based on ignoring the reasons people might feel despair about the future of the UK or the wider world. Instead, he sees hope as the belief that change remains possible even when its timing and shape are unclear: joy after mourning, beauty from the ashes, and the sense that solid ground may eventually be found.

Music offers him the clearest evidence. Songs shaped by suffering can become sources of collective joy. He points to Fela Kuti’s song about his mother’s execution, the grime that emerged from hardship in council estates, and calypso’s roots in the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade. Across different places and eras, he sees artistic creation as a way of moving from pain towards joy.

That idea runs through the guest edit: stories, artists and experiences that help people hold on to a more positive outlook. Koleoso’s own selection is joined by cultural recommendations from his Ezra Collective bandmates.

items: Femi Koleoso guest-edits the Saturday culture section.
He describes hope as the possibility of renewal after pain.
Music, film and shared cultural experiences form the guest edit’s emotional centre.

blocks.text: Among the recommendations are Kleber Mendonça Filho’s film The Secret Agent, praised by TJ Koleoso for its intensity and immersive portrait of 1970s Brazil; Rosa Passos’s album Recriação, chosen by Joe Armon-Jones for its spare, precise instrumentation; and the Southbank Centre, selected by Koleoso after its steelpan celebrations brought generations and cultures together.

Ife Ogunjobi recommends Akinola Davies Jr’s 2025 film My Father’s Shadow, a Nigerian coming-of-age story whose rawness and cultural depth resonated with him. James Mollison chooses KeiyaA’s Hooke’s Law, admiring its shifting sound worlds and the fact that the artist produced the entire album herself.

For Koleoso, hope is not a promise that pain will disappear. It is the possibility that pain can be transformed — through music, shared experience and the creative work that helps people imagine joy again.

Conservative and Reform candidates hope to draw voters away from Labour as parties begin positioning themselves for the 2028 contest.
The contest to become London’s mayor is beginning to take shape, although Sadiq Khan has not yet said whether he will seek another term. The three-time mayor has said he will decide next year.

items: A Savanta UK poll put Labour on 33%, the Conservatives and Reform UK on 18% each, and the Greens on 17%.

“The race is Khan’s to lose, at the moment.”

blocks.text: London mayoral contenders prepare for a race Sadiq Khan is favoured to win

items: A Savanta poll put Labour on 33%, with the Conservatives and Reform UK on 18% each.

blocks.text: The contest to become London’s next mayor is beginning to take shape, although the current mayor, Sadiq Khan, has not confirmed whether he will seek another term in 2028. He has said he will decide next year.

Khan has held the mayoralty since 2016 and remains the candidate to beat. A recent Savanta UK poll for Queen Mary University of London’s Mile End Institute put Labour’s candidate on 33%. The Conservatives and Reform UK were each on 18%, followed by the Greens on 17% and the Liberal Democrats on 9%.

Former home secretary James Cleverly has said he will seek the Conservative nomination. He presented himself as an aspirational, entrepreneurial and forward-looking candidate who understands London, arguing that the city is more pragmatic at elections than its left-leaning reputation suggests.

Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first Black police and crime commissioner, is also standing for the Conservative nomination. He is presenting himself as a fresh face with private-sector experience rather than a former government minister.

The Conservative campaign faces a direct challenge from Reform UK. Laila Cunningham, a former Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor, has been campaigning in London since the start of the year and says she will not step aside for the Conservatives.

Cunningham argues that the right-of-centre vote is divided, but believes Reform can attract some Labour voters. She points to the party’s gains in Barking and Dagenham in the local elections and says her background as the daughter of Egyptian immigrants challenges assumptions about a typical Reform supporter.

Labour MP Dawn Butler has also indicated that she may run. She previously raised the possibility in 2023 and has said she would enter the race if Khan confirms he will not seek a third term. Khan did not respond to a request for comment.

The Greens have not named a clear candidate. The party is currently focused on its leader Zack Polanski’s planned campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, while saying it has several potential mayoral candidates.
For now, the main uncertainty is not who has entered the race but whether Khan will run again—and whether divided opposition parties can turn the contest into a close one.

blocks.text: Earth Garden is built for listening. It lets you explore a globe filled with real field recordings, from waves along remote Atlantic islands to crickets in Tanzania and rain on the streets of Manhattan.

The experience recalls Radio Garden, which connects listeners to live radio stations around the world. Here, the map is driven by environmental sound instead. Set the globe to rotate automatically and the reticle moves between locations, transitioning into new recordings as it travels.
It turns a globe into a map of everyday sounds.

The recordings are sourced from Freesound. That gives Earth Garden a broad and varied library, but it also brings some unevenness: recording quality and volume can differ between clips. The collection is more concentrated in the United States and Europe, particularly the United Kingdom.

There is also an option to add generic ambient drones in the background. Used as background audio, the result can be soothing; used actively, it offers a chance to notice the small details in familiar and distant environments alike.
Earth Garden is a simple, calming way to browse field recordings by place, with Freesound’s variety—and inconsistency—along for the ride.

blocks.text: Tupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the case
Testimony in the conviction of Duane “Keffe D” Davis highlighted how quickly investigators received information about the killing — and why the case remained unresolved for 27 years.

items: Duane “Keffe D” Davis was convicted of orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s killing.
Police heard soon after the shooting that a conflict involving Southside Compton Crips members could have prompted the attack.
Las Vegas police did not make an arrest in the case for 27 years.

blocks.text: The trial brought renewed scrutiny to the long investigation into Shakur’s 1996 murder. Witnesses described missed opportunities, concerns about police corruption and competing priorities between departments, alongside the reluctance of some people close to the case to cooperate with authorities.

Davis, a Southside Compton Crips gang leader and drug dealer, told investigators in 2008 that his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, fired the shots. Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998 and was never charged. Davis’s conviction came after a Las Vegas jury deliberated for less than three hours.
“If even he could be murdered on a major Las Vegas boulevard and the case could sit around and languish, one naturally wonders what happens when the victim is just a 19-year-old Black man.”

The evidence presented at trial suggested that investigators received useful information almost immediately. Reggie Wright Jr, then head of security for Shakur’s record label and a former Compton police officer, said he called his father, a Compton gang-unit commander, after the shooting. He warned that Shakur and Marion “Suge” Knight had recently fought with men linked to the Southside Crips and that violence could follow in Compton.

Robert Ladd, then a Compton gang-homicide detective, testified that officers expected retaliation. Over the following 10 days, three people were killed and 10 attempted murders were reported, including a shooting that critically injured a 10-year-old girl. Ladd said the violence reinforced his belief that Southside Crips members were responsible for Shakur’s death.

Compton police detained gang members, collected firearms and invited Las Vegas detectives to interview people they believed might be involved, including Anderson. Two Las Vegas detectives came to Compton, but Ladd testified that little resulted from the interview. He later said the meeting lasted about 20 minutes and that Las Vegas showed little interest in speaking with the people Compton had identified.

Las Vegas detectives also had reasons to question information coming from Compton. Wright Jr had worked for Knight while still employed as a police officer, and his security business hired off-duty and retired officers to protect Death Row Records. Investigators worried that Compton officers might pass information to Knight or protect him. Wright denied wrongdoing, while he and his father later faced federal drug-trafficking and money-laundering charges.

The trial also showed that witness cooperation was uneven. Shakur reportedly declined to identify his shooter while being treated in an ambulance. Other witnesses feared being branded informers or facing retaliation, and some resisted prosecutors’ questions. Those concerns helped sustain the long-standing explanation that street culture and fear had obstructed the investigation, but the testimony also exposed delays and disagreements within law enforcement itself.

The case resonated beyond the music world because Shakur was one of the most visible Black men in the United States. His death became a lasting example, critics argue, of how the justice system can fail to deliver answers even when a victim is famous and the shooting occurs in public. The trial’s swift verdict has therefore raised a basic question: if evidence existed early, why did resolution take so long?

The conviction resolved the prosecution of Davis, but the testimony left a wider issue unresolved: whether missed leads, institutional distrust and departmental conflict allowed Shakur’s murder to remain unsolved for decades.

blocks.text: Tupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the case
Police received information almost immediately after the killing. It took Las Vegas police 27 years to make an arrest.

items: Duane “Keffe D” Davis was convicted of orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s killing.
Investigators heard allegations about the shooting and its motive soon after it happened.
The trial highlighted disputed police judgments, possible corruption, witness fears and jurisdictional conflict.

blocks.text: For years, US law enforcement officials attributed the failure to solve Tupac Shakur’s murder to uncooperative witnesses and a gang culture summed up by the phrase “snitches get stitches”. Testimony in the long-delayed trial, which concluded this week nearly 30 years after Shakur’s death, presented a more complicated picture: police had received important information almost immediately, yet the case remained unresolved for decades.

A Las Vegas jury convicted Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a Southside Compton Crips gang leader and drug dealer, of orchestrating the killing. Davis told investigators in 2008 that his nephew, Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, had fired the shots. Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998 and was never charged in Shakur’s death.

The case has resonated beyond Shakur’s family and friends, particularly among Black Americans. Jody Armour, a law professor at the University of Southern California, said that if one of the world’s most famous Black men could be killed on a major Las Vegas boulevard while the case languished, it raised questions about what happens to less visible victims. Shakur had spent much of his career arguing that America did not adequately value Black life; his unsolved killing became, Armour said, another example supporting that argument.
“If even he could be murdered on a major Las Vegas boulevard and the case could sit around and languish, one naturally wonders what happens when the victim is just a 19-year-old Black man.”

Mark Chutkow, a former federal prosecutor, said the jury’s decision after less than three hours suggested that the evidence was persuasive enough to support a conviction. It also raised the question of why that evidence had not produced an arrest sooner.

Surveillance footage shown at trial depicted Shakur, Death Row Records founder Marion “Suge” Knight and their associates, some linked to the Mob Piru Bloods, assaulting Anderson at the MGM hotel in Las Vegas. Davis later said the attack prompted him and Anderson to seek revenge.

In the hours after Shakur was shot, Reggie Wright Jr, then head of security for Death Row Records, said he called a Compton police lieutenant several times. Wright warned that Shakur and Knight had fought with men from the Southside Crips and that trouble was likely in Compton. Wright had formerly been a Compton officer and was calling his father, Reginald Wright Sr, who led the department’s gang unit.

The information was passed to Robert Ladd, a Compton gang homicide detective. Ladd testified that officers expected retaliatory violence. Over the next 10 days, three people were killed and 10 others were targeted, including a 10-year-old girl who was left critically injured. Ladd said the violence convinced him that the information identifying Southside Crips members was accurate.

Compton police then detained many local gang members, including Anderson, and invited Las Vegas investigators to interview them. Officers also collected firearms in the hope of finding the murder weapon. Two Las Vegas detectives went to Compton and interviewed Anderson, but Ladd testified that little came of it. He later said the interview lasted about 20 minutes and that Las Vegas police showed no real interest in speaking with the people Compton officers believed were involved.

Anderson was publicly identified as a possible suspect within weeks of the shooting. He, his lawyer and his family denied his involvement, but people close to him later said the accusation shaped his life. In 1997, Shakur’s mother, Afeni Shakur, filed a civil lawsuit accusing Anderson of murdering her son. Nearly three decades later, an audio recording played in court captured Davis identifying Anderson as the shooter.

Las Vegas detectives had reasons to distrust information coming from Compton. The city and its police department had reputations for political corruption, scandals and internal conflict. The department would later be disbanded by the city council. Wright Jr’s role also raised concerns: he had worked for Knight while still a police officer, and his father led Compton’s gang unit. Investigators feared information might be passed to Knight or that he might be protected.

Wright testified that he had grown up in a neighborhood associated with the Mob Piru gang and had known gang members since childhood. His private security company employed off-duty and retired officers to protect Death Row’s studio and artists. One witness, Mob James McDonald, described the close working relationship between Wright’s security staff and the gang members around Knight.

Davis later accused Knight of employing police hitmen and corrupt officers, naming Wright and his father. Both men were subsequently indicted on federal drug-trafficking and money-laundering charges. In the Shakur investigation, the Compton police chief removed Wright Sr from the case in an attempt to address concerns, but the doubts remained. In the absence of an official explanation, conspiracy theories spread, and Wright himself became a potential suspect—an allegation he denied in court.

The trial also confirmed that some witnesses did not want to help prosecutors. A former Las Vegas officer testified that Shakur, while wounded in an ambulance, declined to identify his shooter, saying words to the effect of: “No, we’ll take care of it.” Other witnesses described fears of being labelled informers or facing retaliation. McDonald repeatedly warned prosecutors to treat him as a hostile witness and refused to answer some questions.

At the same time, investigators were divided by their own bureaucratic disputes. Former Los Angeles police detective Greg Kading, who served on a taskforce that heard Davis’s 2008 confession, had initially been assigned to investigate the 1997 killing of Christopher “Biggie Smalls” Wallace. Like Shakur’s murder, that case remained officially unresolved for decades. The overlapping investigations added another layer to a story shaped by rivalry, mistrust and missed opportunities.

The conviction resolved the central criminal case against Davis, but the trial also exposed why the investigation took so long: information arrived early, yet distrust between departments, concerns about police relationships, witness fear and institutional conflict repeatedly obstructed the path to a conclusion.

blocks.text: iPhone Handoff could let two phones share one number
The feature is expected with iOS 27 later this month, although carrier support will be required.

Apple is preparing a feature called iPhone Handoff that would let you switch between two iPhones while keeping the same phone number. It was briefly mentioned during the WWDC keynote in June, but Apple did not explain how it would work.
A demo clip from Xcode 27’s Device Hub now shows the setup. Users can pair two iPhones, designating one as the main device and the other as its companion.
The idea is simple: keep one number available across two phones, rather than moving a SIM or setting up a separate line.

The timing would fit Apple’s expected launch of a foldable iPhone Ultra. Someone carrying a large, expensive phone might prefer to switch temporarily to a smaller or less costly device when they leave home. That could include an older phone that is still in service, even if it has seen better days.
Handoff will depend on carrier support. References to T-Mobile US and Telekom.de have appeared in the code, but wider availability remains unclear.
iPhone Handoff is expected in iOS 27 and could pair two iPhones around one number, but its usefulness will depend on which carriers support it.

blocks.text: CD sales are booming as physical media stages a comeback
Compact discs are selling sharply more than a year ago, even as streaming remains the dominant way people listen to music.

items: 17.5 million CDs were sold in the first half of 2026, according to the RIAA, up 45.7% from the same period in 2025.
CD revenue reached $171.1 million, while vinyl sales rose nearly 21% to 26.5 million units.
Streaming revenue still grew 4.7% to $4.9 billion, far exceeding physical-media sales combined.

blocks.text: CD sales have made an unexpected return. The Recording Industry Association of America said 17.5 million discs were sold in the first six months of 2026, compared with 12 million during the same period last year. Revenue rose 58.6%, reaching $171.1 million.

The increase is striking partly because CD sales fell 22% between 2024 and 2025. Another research firm, Luminate, also recorded strong growth, reporting 16.3 million units sold in the first half of 2026.
For many buyers, a CD is no longer only something to play. It can also be something to keep.

Luminate suggested that special-edition releases from K-pop acts such as BTS helped drive the change. Gen Z and millennial buyers may be treating CDs more like collectibles: the firm said only about half of purchasers owned a CD player.

Other physical formats are growing too. Vinyl sales climbed nearly 21% year on year to 26.5 million units, while a broader category including CD singles, DVDs, cassettes and other formats rose more than 73% to 1.6 million units.

The renewed interest in discs, records and even older digital players does not mean listeners are abandoning streaming. Streaming revenue grew 4.7% to $4.9 billion, still dwarfing physical media as a whole.
Physical music is finding a new role as merchandise, memorabilia and a more tangible way to connect with an artist. Streaming, meanwhile, remains the everyday default for most listening.

blocks.text: CD sales are booming as physical media continues its resurgence
CD purchases rose sharply in the first half of 2026, even as streaming remained the music industry's dominant business.

items: 17.5 million CDs were sold in the US in the first half of 2026, according to the RIAA.
CD sales revenue reached $171.1 million, up 58.6% from the same period in 2025.
Streaming revenue grew to $4.9 billion, far exceeding all physical-media sales combined.

blocks.text: CD sales in the US rose 45.7% year over year in the first six months of 2026, according to a new report from the Recording Industry Association of America. The increase follows a 22% decline between 2024 and 2025, making the rebound especially striking.

The figures are not identical across industry reports. Research firm Luminate counted 16.3 million units sold during the same period. It attributed much of the growth to special editions from K-pop acts such as BTS, with Gen Z and millennial buyers often treating CDs as collectibles; Luminate said only about half of buyers owned a CD player.

Other physical formats are growing too. Vinyl sales increased nearly 21% to 26.5 million units, while a broader category including CD singles, DVDs, cassettes, SACD and DVD-Audio rose more than 73% to 1.6 million units.
Physical media is growing, but streaming still defines the market.

The resurgence does not mean listeners are abandoning streaming. Streaming revenue rose 4.7% to $4.9 billion, dwarfing revenue from physical formats combined. The pattern points to physical music serving a different role: part listening format, part collectible, and part connection to an artist or release.
CDs are having a notable comeback, driven in part by collectible editions, while streaming remains the industry’s financial center.
